She reports prolonged bleeding after minor cuts and has noticed easy bruising. On physical examination, multiple small bruises are on her arms and legs. Which of the following tests is most likely to be abnormal?
questions.solution: a primary hemostasis defect (platelet dysfunction or vWD). Bleeding Time (BT): Prolonged when platelet number or function is reduced → best screening test for primary hemostasis defect. Clotting Time (CT) (Option B) : Measures overall clot formation (intrinsic + extrinsic); normal in isolated platelet defects. Normal CT: 8-15 mins. Prothrombin Time (PT) (Option C): Prolonged only in extrinsic pathway disorders (factor VII deficiency, warfarin therapy). Normal PT: 11-16 secs. Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT) (Option D): Prolonged in intrinsic pathway defects (hemophilia A/B, heparin therapy). Normal aPTT: 25-30 secs. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
a primary hemostasis defect (platelet dysfunction or vWD).

Bleeding Time (BT):

  • Prolonged when platelet number or function is reduced → best screening test for primary hemostasis defect.

Clotting Time (CT) (Option B):

  • Measures overall clot formation (intrinsic + extrinsic); normal in isolated platelet defects. 
  • Normal CT: 8-15 mins.

Prothrombin Time (PT) (Option C):

  • Prolonged only in extrinsic pathway disorders (factor VII deficiency, warfarin therapy). 
  • Normal PT: 11-16 secs.

Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT) (Option D):

  • Prolonged in intrinsic pathway defects (hemophilia A/B, heparin therapy). 
  • Normal aPTT: 25-30 secs.

questions.stem: Which of the following age groups is a greenstick fracture most commonly observed?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following age groups is a greenstick fracture most commonly observed?
questions.solution: ctures where the bone bends and cracks on one side without breaking completely. They are most common in children due to their growing bones, which have a higher cartilage content, making them more pliable. The presence of epiphyseal plates (growth plates) allows children's bones to bend under stress instead of breaking entirely. Greenstick Fracture Definition A greenstick fracture is an incomplete fracture commonly seen in children, where one cortex of the bone is broken while the other cortex remains intact, resembling the bending and partial breaking of a young, flexible bamboo. Common Sites Most Common Fracture in Children: Occurs before epiphyseal closure, predominantly in children aged 4 to 10 years. Most Affected Bone: Typically involves the forearm bones (radius and ulna). Clinical Features Patients often present with pain, tenderness, and swelling over the affected area. There may be a limitation in the range of motion. The mechanism of injury often involves a fall or a direct blow to the arm. Diagnosis X-ray: Shows a small opening or a line at one cortex with the other cortex remaining intact. {{caption_text}} Radiographic appearance resembles a bending of the bone rather than a complete break. @Neet_pg_bot

ctures where the bone bends and cracks on one side without breaking completely.
  • They are most common in children due to their growing bones, which have a higher cartilage content, making them more pliable.
  • The presence of epiphyseal plates (growth plates) allows children's bones to bend under stress instead of breaking entirely.

    Greenstick Fracture

    Definition

    A greenstick fracture is an incomplete fracture commonly seen in children, where one cortex of the bone is broken while the other cortex remains intact, resembling the bending and partial breaking of a young, flexible bamboo.

    Common Sites
    • Most Common Fracture in Children: Occurs before epiphyseal closure, predominantly in children aged 4 to 10 years.
    • Most Affected Bone: Typically involves the forearm bones (radius and ulna).

    Clinical Features
    • Patients often present with pain, tenderness, and swelling over the affected area.
    • There may be a limitation in the range of motion.
    • The mechanism of injury often involves a fall or a direct blow to the arm.

    Diagnosis
    • X-ray: Shows a small opening or a line at one cortex with the other cortex remaining intact.
    • Radiographic appearance resembles a bending of the bone rather than a complete break.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old male presents with symptoms of acute onset blurred vision, dry mouth, tachycardia, and urinary retention. His medical history is unremarkable, and he denies any recent illnesses or medication use. On examination, his pupils are dilated and unreactive to light. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his presentation?
questions.stemHtml: A 34-year-old male presents with symptoms of acute onset blurred vision, dry mouth, tachycardia, and urinary retention. His medical history is unremarkable, and he denies any recent illnesses or medication use. On examination, his pupils are dilated and unreactive to light. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his presentation?
questions.solution: opine poisoning (Belladonna poisoning): Atropine is an anticholinergic medication that blocks the action of acetylcholine in the body by binding to muscarinic receptors. In cases of overdose or poisoning, it can cause dry mouth, blurred vision, tachycardia, urinary retention, and dilated pupils, among others. It is treated with physostigmine, which increases ACh levels; it can even cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB) to reverse the CNS effects of atropine poisoning. Cocaine toxicity (Option A): Here the patient is hyperexcitable with tachycardia due to sympathetic discharge. Opioids (Option B): Here, the pupils are not dilated; rather, they are constricted or miotic. Benzodiazepines (Option C): Here, the hallmark feature is respiratory depression . @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
opine poisoning (Belladonna poisoning):
  • Atropine is an anticholinergic medication that blocks the action of acetylcholine in the body by binding to muscarinic receptors.
  • In cases of overdose or poisoning, it can cause dry mouth, blurred vision, tachycardia, urinary retention, and dilated pupils, among others.
  • It is treated with physostigmine, which increases ACh levels; it can even cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB) to reverse the CNS effects of atropine poisoning.

 

Cocaine toxicity (Option A): Here the patient is hyperexcitable with tachycardia due to sympathetic discharge.  

Opioids (Option B): Here, the pupils are not dilated; rather, they are constricted or miotic. 

Benzodiazepines (Option C): Here, the hallmark feature is respiratory depression.

questions.stem: Which of the following agents inhibits the action of an agonist on a receptor or the subsequent response but does not have any effect of its own?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following agents inhibits the action of an agonist on a receptor or the subsequent response but does not have any effect of its own?
questions.solution: Correct Answer: C) Drug C Drug C (Option C) : Antagonist It prevents the action of an agonist on a receptor or the subsequent response, but does not have any effect of its own. E.g. Naloxone, an opioid receptor antagonist Drug A (Option A) : Agonist It activates a receptor to produce an effect similar to the physiological signal molecule (e.g., morphine at opioid receptors). Drug D (Option D) : Inverse Agonist It activates a receptor to produce an effect opposite to that of an agonist (e.g., Rimonabant at cannabinoid receptors). Drug B (Option B) : Partial Agonist It activates a receptor to produce a submaximal effect and can block the action of a full agonist (e.g., Buprenorphine at opioid receptors). Super Agonist Not directly relevant to opioid overdose treatment but produces a maximum response greater than that of the endogenous agonist (e.g., BMS-986121 at GLP-1 receptors). @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Answer: C) Drug C

Drug C (Option C): Antagonist


 
  • It prevents the action of an agonist on a receptor or the subsequent response, but does not have any effect of its own. 
  • E.g. Naloxone, an opioid receptor antagonist

Drug A (Option A): Agonist

 
  • It activates a receptor to produce an effect similar to the physiological signal molecule (e.g., morphine at opioid receptors).

Drug D (Option D): Inverse Agonist


 
  • It activates a receptor to produce an effect opposite to that of an agonist (e.g., Rimonabant at cannabinoid receptors).

Drug B (Option B): Partial Agonist
  • It activates a receptor to produce a submaximal effect and can block the action of a full agonist (e.g., Buprenorphine at opioid receptors).

Super Agonist
  • Not directly relevant to opioid overdose treatment but produces a maximum response greater than that of the endogenous agonist (e.g., BMS-986121 at GLP-1 receptors).

diagnosis in this clinical presentation is Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD), a prion disease.

 

Prion Disease or Transmissible Spongiform Encephalopathy (TSE):

  • Prions are proteinaceous infectious particles with no RNA/DNA.
  • Pathogenesis: Misfolding of normal prion protein (PrPc) to form beta-pleated configuration (PrPSc).
  • Histopathology: Spongiform vacuolisation inside the cell.
  • Associated diseases:

Types of prion disease
1. Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (M/C)

  • Genetic: Familial form caused by PRNP mutation.
  • Transmission: Iatrogenic
  • Symptoms:
    • Dementia.
    • Associated pronounced involuntary jerking muscle contractions on sudden stimulation (startle myoclonus) and cerebellar dysfunction (ataxia).
  • Histopathogenesis:
    • Spongiform transformation of the cerebral cortex.
  • Prognosis: Uniformly fatal with average survival < 7 months after the onset of symptoms.

2. Kuru disease

  • PAS & Congo: red positive.
  • Kuru plaques: Extracellular aggregated abnormal PrP.

3. Fatal familial insomnia

4. Bovine spongiform encephalopathy

questions.solution: ="1" cellspacing="1" style="width:100%"> Medical management of Glaucoma Topical drugs Beta-blockers: Decrease the formation of aqueous humour. Eg: Timolol, betaxolol Alpha agonists: Have dual action i.e. they decrease the formation of aqueous and increase the trabecular outflow. Eg: Adrenaline/epinephrine, dipivefrin, brimonidine, and apraclonidine Miotics: These increase the trabecular outflow and open the angle blockage. ="1" cellspacing="1" style="width:100%"> Medical management of Glaucoma Topical drugs

questions.stem: In a Lineweaver-Burk plot for an enzyme experiencing non-competitive inhibition, which of the following statements is correct?
questions.stemHtml: In a Lineweaver-Burk plot for an enzyme experiencing non-competitive inhibition, which of the following statements is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The slope of the Lineweaver-Burk plot increases, but the y-intercept remains the same.

options.label: B
options.text: The y-intercept increases while Km remains constant and the slope increases.

options.label: C
options.text: Both the slope and the y-intercept increase.

options.label: D
options.text: The slope of the Lineweaver-Burk plot decreases while the y-intercept increases.

questions.answerText: The y-intercept increases while Km remains constant and the slope increases.
questions.solution: mMeta" data-dictid="b5fb56a28b1692777190396ae8b625">inhibitor binds to an enzyme at a site other than the active site, which is called an allosteric site. This binding changes the enzyme's shape and reduces its activity, regardless of whether the substrate is present. Effect on the Lineweaver-Burk Plot: The lineweaver burk plot is graphical representation of enzyme kinetics representing Vmax and Km. Effect on Vmax: The y-intercept of the Lineweaver-Burk plot, which represents 1/Vmax increases as Vmax decreases. Effect on Km: The slope of the plot, which is Km/Vmax, remains constant because Km does not change. The y-intercept increases while the Km remains constant for non competitive inhibition. Examples of non-competitive inhibitors: Cyanide acts as a non-competitive inhibitor by binding to a site on cytochrome c oxidase that is not the active site, thereby disrupting its function. Fluoride functions as a non-competitive inhibitor by chelating essential metal ions (magnesium or manganese) required for enolase activity, thus inhibiting the enzyme. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
mMeta" data-dictid="b5fb56a28b1692777190396ae8b625">inhibitor binds to an enzyme at a site other than the active site, which is called an allosteric site. This binding changes the enzyme's shape and reduces its activity, regardless of whether the substrate is present.

 

Effect on the Lineweaver-Burk Plot:

 

The lineweaver burk plot is graphical representation of enzyme kinetics representing Vmax and Km.

  • Effect on Vmax: The y-intercept of the Lineweaver-Burk plot, which represents 1/Vmax increases as Vmax decreases.
  • Effect on Km: The slope of the plot, which is Km/Vmax, remains constant because Km does not change.

 

The y-intercept increases while the Km remains constant for non competitive inhibition.

 

 

Examples of non-competitive inhibitors:

  • Cyanide acts as a non-competitive inhibitor by binding to a site on cytochrome c oxidase that is not the active site, thereby disrupting its function.
  • Fluoride functions as a non-competitive inhibitor by chelating essential metal ions (magnesium or manganese) required for enolase activity, thus inhibiting the enzyme.

questions.stem: During a vaginal breech delivery, you encounter a case where one of the baby's arms is extended behind the fetal head, causing difficulty in delivery. What technique is used to manage extended arms in this breech delivery scenario?
questions.stemHtml: During a vaginal breech delivery, you encounter a case where one of the baby's arms is extended behind the fetal head, causing difficulty in delivery. What technique is used to manage extended arms in this breech delivery scenario?
questions.solution: "9a1e50b8221692777201b95b66c9de">vaginal breech delivery scenario where one of the baby's arms is extended behind the fetal head, causing difficulty in delivery, the technique typically used to manage this situation is Lovset's manoeuvre. Principle: Due to the curved birth canal, one shoulder remains above the pubic bone while the other is below the sacral promontory. Rotating the fetal trunk with the back anterior and applying downward traction brings the posterior shoulder below the symphysis pubis. Procedure: Lift the baby, induce lateral flexion, rotate the trunk 180° to bring the posterior arm under the pubic arch, and hook out. Rotate the trunk opposite, keeping the back anterior, to deliver the anterior shoulder under the symphysis pubis. Classical manoeuvre (Option A): This typically involves bringing down an arm extended alongside the fetal head to facilitate delivery. It is a traditional method used in breech deliveries, but it may be challenging if the arm is positioned behind the head. Pinard's manoeuvre (Option C): This manoeuvre resolves shoulder dystocia by applying pressure to the anterior shoulder to rotate it internally or manipulate it for delivery. It may be used in some breech deliveries but is not specifically for managing extended arms. Duhrssen's incision (Option D): This refers to a surgical incision made in the cervix or lower uterine segment to facilitate delivery in cases of severe obstruction or dystocia. It is not directly related to managing extended arms in breech deliveries. @Neet_pg_bot

options.text: Excessive use of vitamin D preparations and phosphate binders

options.label: B
options.text: Less use of vitamin D preparations and phosphate binders

questions.answerText: Excessive use of vitamin D preparations and phosphate binders
questions.solution: >Adynamic bone disease is a type of CKD–mineral bone disorder characterized by low bone turnover due to markedly reduced osteoblast and osteoclast activity. The main cause is over-suppression of PTH , often iatrogenic. This occurs with: High-dose vitamin D analogs (calcitriol, alfacalcidol) → suppress PTH secretion Calcium-containing phosphate binders (e.g., calcium acetate, calcium carbonate) → induce hypercalcemia and further suppress PTH Net effect: bone becomes metabolically inactive, unable to remodel → fracture risk and vascular calcification increase . @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
>Adynamic bone disease is a type of CKD–mineral bone disorder characterized by low bone turnover due to markedly reduced osteoblast and osteoclast activity.

  • The main cause is over-suppression of PTH, often iatrogenic.

  • This occurs with:

    • High-dose vitamin D analogs (calcitriol, alfacalcidol) → suppress PTH secretion

    • Calcium-containing phosphate binders (e.g., calcium acetate, calcium carbonate) → induce hypercalcemia and further suppress PTH

  • Net effect: bone becomes metabolically inactive, unable to remodel → fracture risk and vascular calcification increase.

questions.solution: 6927772020efa386e3e">fetal reduction is generally considered for the donor twin in the management of Twin-to-Twin Transfusion Syndrome (TTTS), so as to improve the survival chances of the recipient twin. Twin-to-Twin Transfusion Syndrome (TTTS) Definition TTTS is characterized by deep AV anastomosis between monochorionic twins. More common in MCDA>MCMA Clinical Findings Donor Twin : Oligohydramnios (<2 cm), anemia, hypovolemia, hypotension, growth restriction, "stuck" appearance. Recipient Twin : Polyhydramnios (>8 cm), polycythemia, hypervolemia, hypertension, larger size, risk of heart failure and hydrops fetalis. Diagnostic Criteria Ultrasound Findings : MCDA twin pregnancy, discrepant amniotic fluid volumes, size discrepancy. Doppler Studies : Abnormal blood flow patterns, such as absent or reversed end-diastolic flow in the donor twin's umbilical artery. questions.solutionHtml:
6927772020efa386e3e">fetal reduction is generally considered for the donor twin in the management of Twin-to-Twin Transfusion Syndrome (TTTS), so as to improve the survival chances of the recipient twin.

Twin-to-Twin Transfusion Syndrome (TTTS)

Definition
  • TTTS is characterized by deep AV anastomosis between monochorionic twins.
  • More common in MCDA>MCMA

Clinical Findings
  • Donor Twin: Oligohydramnios (<2 cm), anemia, hypovolemia, hypotension, growth restriction, "stuck" appearance.
  • Recipient Twin: Polyhydramnios (>8 cm), polycythemia, hypervolemia, hypertension, larger size, risk of heart failure and hydrops fetalis.

Diagnostic Criteria
  • Ultrasound Findings: MCDA twin pregnancy, discrepant amniotic fluid volumes, size discrepancy.
  • Doppler Studies: Abnormal blood flow patterns, such as absent or reversed end-diastolic flow in the donor twin's umbilical artery.
  • Hematologic Findings: Hemoglobin difference >5 g%, estimated fetal weight discrepancy >25%.

Management

(Option A, B and D)
  • Laser Ablation
  • Amnioreduction
  • Septostomy
  • Selective Reduction of donor twin

questions.answerText: Administration of oxytocin infusion for at least one hour after delivery
questions.solution: dictid="7e1c459d2b1692777194da47cd13b3">oxytocin infusion for at least one hour after delivery is a crucial step in the active management of the third stage of labor, which can significantly reduce the incidence of PPH. Continuing oxytocin infusion helps maintain uterine contractions and reduces blood loss after delivery. PREVENTION OF PPH Antenatal Measures Intranatal Measures Maintain hemoglobin > 10 gm/dL (Option A) Screen high-risk patients and deliver in well-equipped hospitals Conduct blood grouping for all women Localize the placenta in women with previous cesarean delivery using USG/MRI (Option C) Plan delivery of women with morbidly adherent placenta by a senior obstetrician with blood products ready Active management of the third stage of labor Continue oxytocin infusion for at least one hour after delivery in induced/augmented labor Administer oxytocin 5 IU slow IV during cesarean section (Option B) Use Carbetocin (100 μg IV over 1 min.) to prevent PPH Check the uterovaginal canal for trauma after a difficult labor or instrumental delivery Observe for two hours post-delivery to ensure uterus contraction before transferring to the ward Prefer local or epidural anesthesia over general anesthesia in forceps, ventouse, or breech delivery Allow spontaneous placental separation during cesarean section to reduce blood loss Examine the placenta and membranes routinely for completeness @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
dictid="7e1c459d2b1692777194da47cd13b3">oxytocin infusion for at least one hour after delivery is a crucial step in the active management of the third stage of labor, which can significantly reduce the incidence of PPH. Continuing oxytocin infusion helps maintain uterine contractions and reduces blood loss after delivery.

 

PREVENTION OF PPH

Antenatal Measures

Intranatal Measures
  • Maintain hemoglobin > 10 gm/dL (Option A)
  • Screen high-risk patients and deliver in well-equipped hospitals
  • Conduct blood grouping for all women
  • Localize the placenta in women with previous cesarean delivery using USG/MRI (Option C)
  • Plan delivery of women with morbidly adherent placenta by a senior obstetrician with blood products ready
  • Active management of the third stage of labor
  • Continue oxytocin infusion for at least one hour after delivery in induced/augmented labor
  • Administer oxytocin 5 IU slow IV during cesarean section (Option B)
  • Use Carbetocin (100 μg IV over 1 min.) to prevent PPH
  • Check the uterovaginal canal for trauma after a difficult labor or instrumental delivery
  • Observe for two hours post-delivery to ensure uterus contraction before transferring to the ward
  • Prefer local or epidural anesthesia over general anesthesia in forceps, ventouse, or breech delivery
  • Allow spontaneous placental separation during cesarean section to reduce blood loss
  • Examine the placenta and membranes routinely for completeness

The parents are paint factory workers living in an industrial complex. The child’s urine is noted to be dark red in color. Laboratory tests confirm elevated levels of porphyrins in the blood. Which of the following statements about the diagnosis is incorrect?

options.label: A
options.text: The condition can occur due to exposure to lead, leading to decreased activity of ALA synthase.

options.label: B
options.text: The red fluorescence of the teeth under UV light is referred to as erythrodontia, due to emission of 600 nm wavelength by porphyrin.

options.label: C
options.text: Porphyrin has a specific absorption band called Soret band corresponding to 400 nm.

options.label: D
options.text: Photosensitivity due to the accumulation of porphyrins in the skin which release superoxide radicals causing photooxidative damage.

questions.answerText: The condition can occur due to exposure to lead, leading to decreased activity of ALA synthase.
questions.solution: ion described is more likely a type of porphyria, which involves elevated porphyrins and can occur due to lead exposure. However, the enzyme ALA synthase is not affected by lead. Lead primarily inhibits 3 enzymes of heme synthesis: Ferrochelatase ALA dehydratase Copro-porphyrinogen oxidase Option B: The 4 pyrrole rings in Porphyrins are connected by methenyl bridges (double bonds) capable of absorbing light at 400 nm and emitting light at 600 nm. This 600 nm wavelength appears as the red fluorescence of the teeth under UV light, which is referred to as Erythrodontia . This property of porphyrins is being used in cancer phototherapy Since tumors often take up more porphyrins than do normal tissues, hematoporphyrin or related compounds are administered to a patient with an appropriate tumor. The tumor is then exposed to an argon laser to excite the porphyrins, producing cytotoxic effects. The light absorbed by porphyrins has a specific absorption band called the Soret band (Option C) , which corresponds to around 400 nm as seen on spectrometry. Photosensitivity in porphyria is due to the accumulation of porphyrins in the skin (Option D). Porphyrins absorb light of shorter wavelengths (higher energy) and emit longer wavelengths (lower energy), which in turn releases superoxide radicals causing photooxidative damage. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
ion described is more likely a type of porphyria, which involves elevated porphyrins and can occur due to lead exposure. However, the enzyme ALA synthase is not affected by lead.

Lead primarily inhibits 3 enzymes of heme synthesis:

  • Ferrochelatase
  • ALA dehydratase
  • Copro-porphyrinogen oxidase

 

Option B:

  • The 4 pyrrole rings in Porphyrins are connected by methenyl bridges (double bonds) capable of absorbing light at 400 nm and emitting light at 600 nm.
  • This 600 nm wavelength appears as the red fluorescence of the teeth under UV light, which is referred to as Erythrodontia. This property of porphyrins is being used in cancer phototherapy

 

  • Since tumors often take up more porphyrins than do normal tissues, hematoporphyrin or related compounds are administered to a patient with an appropriate tumor. The tumor is then exposed to an argon laser to excite the porphyrins, producing cytotoxic effects.


 

The light absorbed by porphyrins has a specific absorption band called the Soret band (Option C), which corresponds to around 400 nm as seen on spectrometry.

 

 

Photosensitivity in porphyria is due to the accumulation of porphyrins in the skin (Option D). Porphyrins absorb light of shorter wavelengths (higher energy) and emit longer wavelengths (lower energy), which in turn releases superoxide radicals causing photooxidative damage.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old male presented with cough and breathing difficulty and was diagnosed with emphysema after radiographic examination. Which of the following genetic conditions should be suspected as a possible cause?
questions.stemHtml: A 20-year-old male presented with cough and breathing difficulty and was diagnosed with emphysema after radiographic examination. Which of the following genetic conditions should be suspected as a possible cause?
questions.solution: a-1 antitrypsin deficiency is a genetic condition characterised by low levels or dysfunctional alpha-1 antitrypsin protein. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency: It is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the alpha-1 antitrypsin gene located on Chromosome 14 . The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to panacinar emphysema and the liver, causing cirrhosis due to abnormal protein accumulation. Cystic fibrosis (Option A) is a genetic disorder caused by CFTR gene mutations, leading to thick mucus, chronic lung infections, and bronchiectasis. While it causes obstructive lung disease, emphysema is not typical. Asthma (Option B) is a chronic inflammatory condition causing reversible airway obstruction and episodic wheezing, coughing, and breathlessness. It does not typically result in emphysema or structural lung damage. Bronchiectasis (Option D) is a condition of permanently dilated bronchi due to chronic infections or inflammation. While it causes cough and sputum production, it does not primarily lead to emphysema. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
a-1 antitrypsin deficiency is a genetic condition characterised by low levels or dysfunctional alpha-1 antitrypsin protein.

 

Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency:

  • It is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the alpha-1 antitrypsin gene located on Chromosome 14.
  • The condition primarily affects the lungs, leading to panacinar emphysema and the liver, causing cirrhosis due to abnormal protein accumulation.

 

Cystic fibrosis (Option A) is a genetic disorder caused by CFTR gene mutations, leading to thick mucus, chronic lung infections, and bronchiectasis.

  • While it causes obstructive lung disease, emphysema is not typical.

 

Asthma (Option B) is a chronic inflammatory condition causing reversible airway obstruction and episodic wheezing, coughing, and breathlessness.

  • It does not typically result in emphysema or structural lung damage.

 

Bronchiectasis (Option D) is a condition of permanently dilated bronchi due to chronic infections or inflammation.

  • While it causes cough and sputum production, it does not primarily lead to emphysema.

In a recent census survey conducted in a developing country, the government aims to measure the literacy levels among its population accurately. The survey team decides to calculate both the crude literacy rate and the effective literacy rate to gain a comprehensive understanding.
What distinguishes the effective literacy rate from the crude literacy rate?

questions.solution: g> Hepatitis A is a self-limiting viral infection, especially in children. Management typically involves supportive care, including maintaining hydration and monitoring liver function. Hepatitis A: Etiology: Hepatitis A Virus (HAV) is an RNA virus from the Picornavirus family. Epidemiology: HAV is highly contagious, transmitted primarily through the fecal-oral route. Incubation period: ~3 weeks. Contagious (viral shedding) from late in the incubation period until about 2 weeks after the onset of jaundice. Clinical Manifestations: HAV causes acute hepatitis only. Often anicteric in young children, but symptomatic in older adolescents, adults, and immunocompromised patients. Symptoms : Acute febrile illness with abrupt onset of anorexia, nausea, malaise, vomiting, and jaundice. Duration of illness: 7-14 days. Category Details Diagnosis Anti-HAV IgM antibodies: Detectable during symptoms and remains positive for 4-6 months. Anti-HAV IgG antibodies: Provides long-term immunity and appears within 8 weeks of symptom onset. Elevated levels: ALT, AST, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, 5′-nucleotidase, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase. Complications Full recovery is typical. Acute liver failure (ALF): Rare, particularly in older adolescents, adults, and immunocompromised patients. Prolonged cholestatic syndrome: Leads to pruritus and fat malabsorption, resolves without long-term effects. Acute Relapsing Hepatitis Fulminant hepatitis (Acute Hepatitis E > A) Treatment Supportive care: Intravenous hydration, antipruritic agents, and fat-soluble vitamin supplementation for cholestatic disease. Monitor for signs of ALF. Prevention Vaccine: Two inactivated vaccines, administered intramuscularly in a 2-dose schedule (second dose 6-12 months after the first). Recommended for children >12 months. Isolation: Infected individuals should be isolated for 2 weeks before and 1 week after jaundice onset. Hand hygiene. Immunoglobulin (Ig) Prophylaxis: For preexposure and postexposure prophylaxis, especially in children <12 months, immunocompromised individuals, those with chronic liver disease, and those allergic to the vaccine. Prognosis Excellent prognosis with no long-term sequelae. Start antiviral therapy (Option A): Hepatitis A virus (HAV) infection typically does not require antiviral therapy. The treatment is generally supportive as the infection is usually self-limiting. Administer Hepatitis A vaccine (Option B): The vaccine is used for prevention, not for treatment of an acute infection. Since the patient already has a positive Anti-HAV IgM, indicating an acute infection, the vaccine is not appropriate in this context. Admit for immediate liver biopsy (Option D): A liver biopsy is not indicated in the acute phase of Hepatitis A. The diagnosis is based on clinical presentation and serology, and a biopsy is not necessary for routine management of this infection. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
g>

Hepatitis A is a self-limiting viral infection, especially in children. Management typically involves supportive care, including maintaining hydration and monitoring liver function.

 

Hepatitis A:

 

Etiology: Hepatitis A Virus (HAV) is an RNA virus from the Picornavirus family.

 

Epidemiology:

  • HAV is highly contagious, transmitted primarily through the fecal-oral route.
  • Incubation period: ~3 weeks.
  • Contagious (viral shedding) from late in the incubation period until about 2 weeks after the onset of jaundice.

 

Clinical Manifestations:

  • HAV causes acute hepatitis only.
  • Often anicteric in young children, but symptomatic in older adolescents, adults, and immunocompromised patients.
  • Symptoms: Acute febrile illness with abrupt onset of anorexia, nausea, malaise, vomiting, and jaundice.

Duration of illness: 7-14 days.

 

Category

Details

Diagnosis
  • Anti-HAV IgM antibodies: Detectable during symptoms and remains positive for 4-6 months.
  • Anti-HAV IgG antibodies: Provides long-term immunity and appears within 8 weeks of symptom onset.
  • Elevated levels: ALT, AST, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, 5′-nucleotidase, γ-glutamyl transpeptidase.

Complications
  • Full recovery is typical.
  • Acute liver failure (ALF): Rare, particularly in older adolescents, adults, and immunocompromised patients.
  • Prolonged cholestatic syndrome: Leads to pruritus and fat malabsorption, resolves without long-term effects.
  • Acute Relapsing Hepatitis
  • Fulminant hepatitis (Acute Hepatitis E > A)

Treatment
  • Supportive care: Intravenous hydration, antipruritic agents, and fat-soluble vitamin supplementation for cholestatic disease.
  • Monitor for signs of ALF.

Prevention
  • Vaccine: Two inactivated vaccines, administered intramuscularly in a 2-dose schedule (second dose 6-12 months after the first). Recommended for children >12 months.
  • Isolation: Infected individuals should be isolated for 2 weeks before and 1 week after jaundice onset.
  • Hand hygiene.
  • Immunoglobulin (Ig) Prophylaxis: For preexposure and postexposure prophylaxis, especially in children <12 months, immunocompromised individuals, those with chronic liver disease, and those allergic to the vaccine.

Prognosis
  • Excellent prognosis with no long-term sequelae.

 

 

 

Start antiviral therapy (Option A): Hepatitis A virus (HAV) infection typically does not require antiviral therapy. The treatment is generally supportive as the infection is usually self-limiting.

 

Administer Hepatitis A vaccine (Option B): The vaccine is used for prevention, not for treatment of an acute infection. Since the patient already has a positive Anti-HAV IgM, indicating an acute infection, the vaccine is not appropriate in this context.

 

Admit for immediate liver biopsy (Option D): A liver biopsy is not indicated in the acute phase of Hepatitis A. The diagnosis is based on clinical presentation and serology, and a biopsy is not necessary for routine management of this infection.

Considering 2 grams of bleaching powder (calcium hypochlorite) is needed per cubic meter of water for effective disinfection, how much bleaching powder is required to disinfect this well?
questions.stemHtml: You are required to disinfect a well using Horrock’s apparatus. The well has a diameter of 1.5 meters and a depth of 10 meters. Considering 2 grams of bleaching powder (calcium hypochlorite) is needed per cubic meter of water for effective disinfection, how much bleaching powder is required to disinfect this well?
questions.solution: n: 1. Calculate the volume of the well : Volume of a cylinder = π × (radius)² × height (or) V= π x (diameter/2)² x height Radius = Diameter / 2 = 1.5 meters / 2 = 0.75 meters Height = Depth of the well = 10 meters Volume = π × (0.75 meters)² × 10 meters → Volume ≈ 3.14 × 0.5625 × 10 → Volume ≈ 17.67 cubic meters 2. Calculate the amount of bleaching powder needed : Bleaching powder required = Volume of the well × Amount of bleaching powder per cubic meter ⇒ 17.67 cubic meters × 2 grams per cubic meter Bleaching powder required ≈ 35.33 grams Rounding off, the required amount of bleaching powder is approximately 35 grams. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
n:

1. Calculate the volume of the well:

  • Volume of a cylinder = π × (radius)² × height (or) V= π x (diameter/2)² x height
  • Radius = Diameter / 2 = 1.5 meters / 2 = 0.75 meters
  • Height = Depth of the well = 10 meters

Volume = π × (0.75 meters)² × 10 meters

→ Volume ≈ 3.14 × 0.5625 × 10

→ Volume ≈ 17.67 cubic meters

2. Calculate the amount of bleaching powder needed:

  • Bleaching powder required = Volume of the well × Amount of bleaching powder per cubic meter

⇒ 17.67 cubic meters × 2 grams per cubic meter

  • Bleaching powder required ≈ 35.33 grams

Rounding off, the required amount of bleaching powder is approximately 35 grams.

questions.solution: nation: The diagnosis in this case is hemochromatosis . Transferrin saturation (TSAT) is the best screening test for hereditary hemochromatosis. Serum ferritin (Option A) is a protein that stores iron in the body. However, while serum ferritin levels can be a useful indicator, they are not as specific as transferrin saturation (TSAT) for diagnosing hemochromatosis. questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital for a routine check-up. During the visit, her diet is discussed, and it is noted that she has been consuming a high carbohydrate diet. You are asked to explain the impact of her dietary habits on glycogen metabolism. Which of the following statements best describes glycogen metabolism?

questions.solutionHtml:
Correct answer B)Reduced peripheral lipolysis

A high-carbohydrate diet increases blood glucose levels, leading to insulin secretion, which promotes glycogen synthesis and suppresses glycogen breakdown. The body enters the fed state, characterized by active glycogenesis and glucose utilization.

  • High glucose levels → Insulin release
  • Insulin stimulates glycogen synthase → Increased glycogen synthesis
  • Inhibits glycogen phosphorylase → Decreased glycogen breakdown.

Glycogen Metabolism in Different Metabolic States

Glycogen metabolism is regulated by the body's metabolic state, primarily influenced by insulin, glucagon, and epinephrine. The balance between glycogenesis (glycogen synthesis) and glycogenolysis (glycogen breakdown) ensures glucose homeostasis.

Metabolic State Primary Hormone Glycogen Metabolism Key Enzymes Involved
Fed State (Option B ruled out) Insulin ↑ Glycogenesis, ↓ Glycogenolysis Glycogen synthase (activated), Glycogen phosphorylase (inhibited)
Fasted State (Option A ruled out) Glucagon ↑ Glycogenolysis, ↓ Glycogenesis Glycogen phosphorylase (activated), Glycogen synthase (inhibited)
Starvation State (Option C ruled out) Glucagon, Cortisol Glycogen nearly depleted, ↑ Gluconeogenesis Gluconeogenic enzymes (e.g., PEPCK, F-1,6-BPase)
Post-Exercise State (Option D ruled out) Epinephrine, Insulin (during recovery) ↑ Glycogenolysis during exercise, ↑ Glycogenesis during recovery Glycogen phosphorylase (exercise), Glycogen synthase (recovery)

Fed State and Glycogenesis (Option B ruled out)

  • After a high-carbohydrate meal, blood glucose levels increase, stimulating insulin secretion from the pancreas.
  • Insulin activates glycogen synthase, promoting the conversion of glucose into glycogen in the liver and muscle.
  • Glycogenolysis is inhibited to store excess glucose.

Fasted State and Glycogenolysis (Option A ruled out)

  • Low blood glucose stimulates glucagon release, which activates glycogen phosphorylase, breaking down glycogen into glucose-1-phosphate.
  • This provides energy for vital functions, primarily in the liver to maintain blood glucose levels.

Starvation State and Gluconeogenesis (Option C ruled out)

  • Glycogen stores are depleted after prolonged fasting.
  • The body shifts to gluconeogenesis, converting amino acids and glycerol into glucose.
  • Cortisol and glucagon drive this process.

Post-Exercise State and Glycogen Replenishment (Option D ruled out)

  • After intense exercise, muscle glycogen is depleted, and the body prioritizes glycogen resynthesis.
  • Insulin sensitivity is high, allowing rapid glucose uptake for glycogenesis in muscle cells.

ass="customMeta" data-dictid="d69566338f1692777189ff10521054">histopathology showing intramacrophagic yeast form and (LPCB) mount showing numerous hyaline hyphae with few tuberculate macroconidia (arrows) and many smooth-walled oval microconidia are pointing towards a diagnosis of disseminated histoplasmosis.

Histoplasmosis

Diagnosis

Microscopy:

  • Stained smears of the specimens show small intra- and extracellular yeast cells
 

Culture:

  • Blood agar and Sabouraud agar show characteristic growth
  • White, cottony, mycelial growth with large, thick-walled, spherical spores with tuberculate (finger-like projections)
 

Serodiagnosis:

  • Antibody titers increase in progressive disease
  • Antigen tests on urine and serum are helpful for immunocompromised individuals.

Skin Test:

  • Delayed hypersensitivity to histoplasmin confirms exposure

Treatment

Amphotericin-B (Option B) for two to four weeks, followed by a year of itraconazole (Option A ruled out)

Fluconazole (Option C ruled out): It is usually reserved for less severe infections or maintenance therapy after initial treatment with more potent antifungals like amphotericin-B. 

Surgical resection (Option D ruled out): It may be considered for localised infections or complications like abscesses, but it is not appropriate as a primary treatment strategy for disseminated histoplasmosis.

questions.stemHtml: What is the mechanism of action of the given drug?
questions.solution: trong>All local anesthetic acts by inhibiting Na+ channels. Mechanism of action & absorption: Site: acts on nodes of ranvier Blocks transmission of pain impulse from nociceptor to spinal cord. Acts on intracellular side of Na channels at inactivation gate blocking the channel. LA doesn’t affect RMP of nerves. Blocks inactivation gates of Na+ channels → Disrupts depolarisation → No action potential generated → No pain sensation. Highest systemic absorption (routes of administration): IV route >Tracheal > Intercostal > Brachial plexus > Epidural. Form for onset of LA action (to reach target nerve) - Unionized form. Active form at site of block of Na channels- Ionized form. Higher doses will act for longer duration and lower doses for a relatively shorter duration. Duration of onset for different local anesthetics (infiltration anesthesia): Short Duration Procaine Chloroprocaine Moderate Duration Lidocaine Prilocaine Long Duration Bupivacaine Ropivacaine Shortest acting - Chloroprocaine Longest acting - Dibucaine Fastest onset - Chloroprocaine (low potency so high concentration used) > Lignocaine (pka is near physiological pH) @Neet_pg_bot

trong>All local anesthetic acts by inhibiting Na+ channels.

Mechanism of action & absorption:

  • Site: acts on nodes of ranvier
  • Blocks transmission of pain impulse from nociceptor to spinal cord.
  • Acts on intracellular side of Na channels at inactivation gate blocking the channel.
  • LA doesn’t affect RMP of nerves.
  • Blocks inactivation gates of Na+ channels → Disrupts depolarisation → No action potential generated → No pain sensation.
  • Highest systemic absorption (routes of administration): IV route >Tracheal > Intercostal > Brachial plexus > Epidural.
  • Form for onset of LA action (to reach target nerve) - Unionized form.
  • Active form at site of block of Na channels- Ionized form.
  • Higher doses will act for longer duration and lower doses for a relatively shorter duration.

 

Duration of onset for different local anesthetics (infiltration anesthesia):

Short Duration
  • Procaine
  • Chloroprocaine

Moderate Duration
  • Lidocaine
  • Prilocaine

Long Duration
  • Bupivacaine
  • Ropivacaine
  • Shortest acting- Chloroprocaine
  • Longest acting- Dibucaine
  • Fastest onset- Chloroprocaine (low potency so high concentration used) > Lignocaine (pka is near physiological pH)

questions.solution: Correct answer-A) Physostigmine This is a case of Myasthenia Gravis, as diurnal variation of neuro-symptoms is seen, and the ice pack test shows resolution of ptosis. Physostigmine crosses the blood-brain barrier and has central action. It has no role in the management of disorders of the peripheral nervous system. Plasma exchange (Option B) & Intravenous immunoglobulins (Option D): IVIg and PLEX would be required if this patient develops Myasthenic crisis. Pyridostigmine (Option C): Pyridostigmine is an anticholinesterase drug that is specifically used to increase acetylcholine activity at the neuromuscular junction, making it the most appropriate treatment for this patient @Neet_pg_bot

Plasma exchange (Option B) & Intravenous immunoglobulins (Option D): IVIg and PLEX would be required if this patient develops Myasthenic crisis.  

Pyridostigmine (Option C): Pyridostigmine is an anticholinesterase drug that is specifically used to increase acetylcholine activity at the neuromuscular junction, making it the most appropriate treatment for this patient

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with chronic liver disease is noted to have elevated blood ammonia on laboratory testing. Which of the following is least likely to result from ammonia neurotoxicity?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man with chronic liver disease is noted to have elevated blood ammonia on laboratory testing. Which of the following is least likely to result from ammonia neurotoxicity?
questions.solution: >rigidity Explanation: Elevated ammonia crosses the blood–brain barrier and is detoxified to glutamine in astrocytes. Excess glutamine increases osmotic pressure , leading to astrocyte swelling, cerebral edema, and impaired neurotransmission . Clinical features of ammonia neurotoxicity: CNS dysfunction manifests as tremors, slurred speech, drowsiness, incoordination, visual disturbances , and in severe cases, coma or death . Rigidity involves extrapyramidal/motor pathways , which are not primarily affected by ammonia. Muscle tone is usually preserved in hyperammonemia, helping differentiate it from conditions like Parkinsonism or tetanus. @Neet_pg_bot

Explanation:

  • Elevated ammonia crosses the blood–brain barrier and is detoxified to glutamine in astrocytes.

    • Excess glutamine increases osmotic pressure, leading to astrocyte swelling, cerebral edema, and impaired neurotransmission.

  • Clinical features of ammonia neurotoxicity: CNS dysfunction manifests as tremors, slurred speech, drowsiness, incoordination, visual disturbances, and in severe cases, coma or death.

  • Rigidity involves extrapyramidal/motor pathways, which are not primarily affected by ammonia.

    • Muscle tone is usually preserved in hyperammonemia, helping differentiate it from conditions like Parkinsonism or tetanus.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old patient undergoes cardiac catheterization with simultaneous ECG recording. During the isovolumic relaxation phase, which combination of events is most accurate?
questions.stemHtml: A 30-year-old patient undergoes cardiac catheterization with simultaneous ECG recording. During the isovolumic relaxation phase, which combination of events is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: T wave ends; ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure; mitral valve opens

options.label: B
options.text: U wave begins; ventricular pressure equals aortic pressure; all valves closed

options.label: C
options.text: P wave starts; ventricular volume increases; tricuspid valve opens

options.label: D
options.text: Second heart sound occurs; ventricular pressure drops rapidly; aortic valve closes

questions.answerText: Second heart sound occurs; ventricular pressure drops rapidly; aortic valve closes
questions.solution: anation : During the isovolumic relaxation phase: It starts with S2 (closure of aortic valve). All valves are closed → no blood enters or leaves. Ventricular pressure falls rapidly as myocardium relaxes. Ventricular volume stays unchanged since valves are shut. T wave (Option A): Ends before isovolumic relaxation. This phase ends when LV pressure falls below LA pressure → mitral valve opens → rapid filling begins. U wave (Option B): Appears after T wave, before P wave. anation :

During the isovolumic relaxation phase:

  • It starts with S2 (closure of aortic valve).

  • All valves are closed → no blood enters or leaves.

  • Ventricular pressure falls rapidly as myocardium relaxes.

  • Ventricular volume stays unchanged since valves are shut.

Bartholin’s Cyst

  • Bartholin's cyst forms when the duct or gland becomes obstructed, leading to fluid buildup.
    • Differential diagnosis:

Tetracycline suspecting chlamydial infection (Option A) and Ampicillin 500 mg 8 hourly (Option B) are both management of Bartholin’s abscess.

Hot compress over the area and analgesics (Option C): Hot compress over the area does reduce the size of the cyst and analgesics have no application as Bartholin cyst is a painless swelling.

questions.stem: RAIU scan was performed for a 35 year old lady with hypertension and palpitations. Diagnosis is?
questions.stemHtml: RAIU scan was performed for a 35 year old lady with hypertension and palpitations. Diagnosis is?
questions.solution: Correct Answer: B) Graves' disease In Graves' disease, there is diffusely increased uptake of radioactive iodine throughout an enlarged gland , often described as a " hot " appearance. Thyroid scan: Thyroid scans use radioactive iodine (I-123) or technetium-99m to assess thyroid function and structure on RAIU scans. Increased uptake indicates hyperfunction, while decreased uptake suggests hypofunction or thyroiditis. The pattern of uptake helps differentiate between diffuse (Graves') and nodular (toxic adenoma, multinodular) causes of hyperthyroidism. Thyroid scans are useful when TSH is suppressed to determine the cause of hyperthyroidism. Interpretation: Normal Thyroid : Uniform uptake throughout the gland. Graves' Disease : Diffusely increased uptake throughout an enlarged gland. Toxic Multinodular Goiter : Multiple areas of increased and decreased uptake. (Option A) Toxic Adenoma : Single area of increased uptake with suppression of surrounding tissue. (Option D) Thyroiditis : Very low or no uptake due to inflammation and destruction of thyroid tissue. (Option C) Thyroid Cancer : Usually appears as "cold" nodules (areas of decreased uptake). @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Answer: B) Graves' disease 

In Graves' disease, there is diffusely increased uptake of radioactive iodine throughout an enlarged gland, often described as a "hot" appearance.

 

Thyroid scan:

  • Thyroid scans use radioactive iodine (I-123) or technetium-99m to assess thyroid function and structure on RAIU scans.
  • Increased uptake indicates hyperfunction, while decreased uptake suggests hypofunction or thyroiditis.
  • The pattern of uptake helps differentiate between diffuse (Graves') and nodular (toxic adenoma, multinodular) causes of hyperthyroidism.
  • Thyroid scans are useful when TSH is suppressed to determine the cause of hyperthyroidism.

 

Interpretation:

  • Normal Thyroid: Uniform uptake throughout the gland.
  • Graves' Disease: Diffusely increased uptake throughout an enlarged gland.
  • Toxic Multinodular Goiter: Multiple areas of increased and decreased uptake. (Option A)
  • Toxic Adenoma: Single area of increased uptake with suppression of surrounding tissue. (Option D)
  • Thyroiditis: Very low or no uptake due to inflammation and destruction of thyroid tissue. (Option C)
  • Thyroid Cancer: Usually appears as "cold" nodules (areas of decreased uptake).

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman is undergoing a gynecological procedure in the lithotomy position. The surgeon is identifying the bony landmarks for access to the pelvic organs. During the examination, the surgeon palpates a bony structure near the midline at the anterior aspect of the perineum. Which of the following bony landmarks is the surgeon most likely palpating?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman is undergoing a gynecological procedure in the lithotomy position. The surgeon is identifying the bony landmarks for access to the pelvic organs. During the examination, the surgeon palpates a bony structure near the midline at the anterior aspect of the perineum. Which of the following bony landmarks is the surgeon most likely palpating?
questions.solution: Explanation: Pubic symphysis is located at the anterior aspect of the perineum and is easily palpated when the patient is in the lithotomy position. View from Lithotomy Position: Bones and Anatomical Landmarks: Pubic Symphysis: Located at the anterior aspect of the pelvis and acts as the anterior boundary of the perineum. Ischiopubic Rami: They form the lateral borders of the urogenital triangle and are important as attachment points for muscles like the ischiocavernosus and the deep and superficial perineal muscles. Ischial Tuberosities: They serve as the lateral borders of the anal triangle. In the lithotomy position, the ischial tuberosities can be palpated as they provide attachment points for the superficial transverse perineal muscles and are important in identifying the perineal body. Coccyx : The small, triangular bone at the base of the spine, forming the posterior border of the pelvic outlet and provides an attachment point for the coccygeus muscle. Sacrum : Lies posteriorly and superiorly, forming the posterior wall of the pelvic cavity. Obturator Foramen: A large opening formed by the pubis and ischium which allows the passage of the obturator nerve and vessels. Perineal Regions Related to Bones: From the lithotomy position, the perineal area can be divided into the urogenital triangle and the anal triangle. Muscles Attached to Bony Landmarks (Visible from Lithotomy Position) : Levator Ani (Pubococcygeus, Iliococcygeus): Support the pelvic organs and form part of the pelvic diaphragm. Ischiocavernosus and Bulbospongiosus: Attach to the ischiopubic rami and help in erection (males) and clitoral function (females). Superficial and Deep Transverse Perineal Muscles: Attach to the ischial tuberosities and the perineal body, providing support to the pelvic floor. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

Pubic symphysis is located at the anterior aspect of the perineum and is easily palpated when the patient is in the lithotomy position.

 

View from Lithotomy Position:

Bones and Anatomical Landmarks:

  • Pubic Symphysis: Located at the anterior aspect of the pelvis and acts as the anterior boundary of the perineum. 
  • Ischiopubic Rami: They form the lateral borders of the urogenital triangle and are important as attachment points for muscles like the ischiocavernosus and the deep and superficial perineal muscles.
  • Ischial Tuberosities: They serve as the lateral borders of the anal triangle. In the lithotomy position, the ischial tuberosities can be palpated as they provide attachment points for the superficial transverse perineal muscles and are important in identifying the perineal body. 
  • Coccyx: The small, triangular bone at the base of the spine, forming the posterior border of the pelvic outlet and provides an attachment point for the coccygeus muscle.
  • Sacrum: Lies posteriorly and superiorly, forming the posterior wall of the pelvic cavity.
  • Obturator Foramen: A large opening formed by the pubis and ischium which allows the passage of the obturator nerve and vessels.

 

Perineal Regions Related to Bones: From the lithotomy position, the perineal area can be divided into the urogenital triangle and the anal triangle.


 

Muscles Attached to Bony Landmarks (Visible from Lithotomy Position):

  • Levator Ani (Pubococcygeus, Iliococcygeus): Support the pelvic organs and form part of the pelvic diaphragm.
  • Ischiocavernosus and Bulbospongiosus: Attach to the ischiopubic rami and help in erection (males) and clitoral function (females).
  • Superficial and Deep Transverse Perineal Muscles: Attach to the ischial tuberosities and the perineal body, providing support to the pelvic floor.

questions.stemHtml: Which muscle is the first to regain function after muscle relaxation?

Meta" data-dictid="59ff8b38191692777201150e72ebc3">Uterine wound dehiscence is a risk of TOLAC 

Vaginal birth after cesarean section (VBAC)

  • Described as vaginal delivery in a woman who has given birth via cesarean section in a former pregnancy.
  • Patients desiring VBAC delivery undergo a trial of labor (TOL), also called the trial of labor after cesarean section (TOLAC).

Selection Criteria of Cases for TOLAC (ACOG)
  • One (RCOG) or two (ACOG) previous lower segment transverse scar.
  • Nonrecurring indication for prior cesarean section.
  • Pelvis adequate for the fetus.
  • Continued labor monitoring possible.
  • Availability of resources (anesthesia, blood transfusion and theatre) for an emergency cesarean section within 30 minutes of the decision.
  • Informed consent of the woman.

 

Contraindications for TOLAC (indications for Cesarean Delivery)
  • Previous classical or inverted T-shaped uterine incision , myomectomy scar
  • Previously >2 LSCS
  • Pelvis contracted or suspected CPD.
  • Presence of other complications in pregnancy: Obstetric (pre-eclampsia, malpresentation, placenta previa) or medical.
  • Resources limited for emergency cesarean delivery or patient refusal for TOLAC.
  • History of prior uterine rupture

 

Benefits of TOLAC

Complications of Unsuccessful TOLAC
  • Decreased maternal morbidity (infection and others).
  • Reduced length of hospital stay. (Option D)
  • Decreased need for blood transfusion.
  • Decreased risk of abnormal placentation (Option A) and need for successive cesarean delivery in next pregnancy. (Option B)
  • Maternal Uterine wound dehiscence. (Option C)
  • Uterine rupture (0.5-1%).
  • Increased blood transfusion.
  • Increased risks of hysterectomy due to uterine rupture.
  • Infections increased maternal morbidity.
  • Perinatal: Low Apgar score, admission to NICU, hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE), neonatal death, rarely stillbirth.

questions.solutionHtml:
data-dictid="66ccee483016927771810c2c295d74">analgesia

Explanation:
Methohexital, which is a barbiturate, does not cause muscle relaxation and does not affect pain perception. It also causes involuntary skeletal muscle contractions.

Methohexital

  • Type: A short-acting barbiturate used for induction of anesthesia. (Option A)
  • Use: commonly administered for procedural sedation and electroconvulsive therapy (ECT).

Mechanism of Action

  • GABA(A) Receptor (Option B): Binds to GABA(A) receptors, enhancing GABA’s effects by increasing the duration of chloride-specific ion channel opening.
  • CNS Effects: Depresses the reticular activating system, leading to decreased consciousness.

Pharmacokinetics

  • Absorption: typically administered intravenously; can also be given rectally in children.
  • Distribution: rapidly crosses the blood-brain barrier due to high lipid solubility; effects seen within 30 seconds.
  • Redistribution: duration of action is primarily determined by redistribution rather than metabolism; typically, plasma levels drop to 10% of peak within 20-30 minutes.
  • Biotransformation: primarily metabolized by the liver to inactive, water-soluble metabolites; clears faster than thiopental.
  • Excretion: excreted mainly in feces; renal excretion is limited.

Clinical Effects

  • CNS depression: induces sedation to unconsciousness based on dosage; can briefly control grand mal seizures (50-100 mg IV). (Option C)
  • Taste sensation: some patients report a garlic or onion-like taste during induction.
  • No pain impairment: does not impair pain perception.
  • Does not cause muscle relaxation but may cause involuntary muscle contractions.

Effects on Organ Systems

  • Cardiovascular: can cause hypotension and tachycardia; effects vary based on administration rate and patient condition.
  • Respiratory: may depress respiratory function; apnea can occur following induction.
  • Cerebral: reduces cerebral blood flow and intracranial pressure; decreases oxygen consumption.
  • Renal: renal blood flow and GFR are reduced.
  • Hepatic: hepatic blood flow is reduced

Drug Interactions

  • CNS Depressants: effects potentiated by ethanol, opioids, and antihistamines.
  • Protein Binding: drugs that occupy protein-binding sites can displace methohexital, increasing free drug levels.

Considerations

  • Dosing: requires careful dosing, particularly in older patients or those with compromised cardiovascular status.
  • Adverse Reactions: sulfonamides reduce the effect of barbiturates, ethanol, opioids, antihistamines and other CNS depressants increase the sedative effect of barbiturates.

Modified Allen Test

Preferred Site for arterial sampling

Radial artery between flexor carpi radialis tendon and styloid process (Option A)

Technique
  • Sequential release allows assessment of individual collateral flow
  • Cannot evaluate collateral circulation if both are released together (Option B)
  • Examines one hand at a time
  • Avoid elbow overextension
  • Palm should initially blanch
  • Normal color should return quickly

Interpretation

Positive Test: (Option C)

• Color returns within 10 seconds → Adequate collateral flow

 

Negative Test:

• Persistent pallor after release → inadequate collateral flow →May need additional testing

• Consider temperature effects

Precaution

Pressure applied on blood sampling site for 5 minutes after sampling is done (Option D) to prevent hematoma

Human epididymal protein 4 (HE4):

  • HE4: > 94% specificity; unaffected by endometriotic cysts
  • Differentiates benign from malignant ovarian tumors
  • Useful for early-stage ovarian cancer detection
  • Elevated in most serous and endometrioid tumors
  • Increased in 50% of clear cell tumors
  • Not elevated in mucinous tumors
  • Combined with CA-125, it detects ovarian and endometrial cancer

Pre-menopausal Predictive Index (PI): 12 + 2.38 x LN(HE4) + 0.0626 x LN (CA-125)

Post-menopausal Predictive Index (PI): 8.09 + 1.04 x LN(HE4) + 0.732 x LN (CA-125)

25.3% postmenopausal women

If life expectancy is 75 years, and death happens at age 30, then 45 years of potential life is lost Proportional mortality rate (Option B) The simplest measure of the burden of disease (Total deaths due to disease 'x'/ Total deaths in a community)́ x 100 Case fatality rate CFR = (Deaths due to diseases ‘z’ / total no of cases of disease ‘z’) x 100 @Neet_pg_bot

-collapse:collapse; width:775px">

Crude death rate

CDR = (Total no. or deaths in a community/ MYP (Mid-year population) in the same area) x 100

  • The mid-year population is taken on 1st July
  • Limitation: It does not consider the age and sex of the population

Age-specific death rate (Option A)

ASDR = (Total no. of deaths in a particular age group (eg. 20-24yrs) a given area in a year/ MYP of the age group in the same area and year) x 1000

Expectation of life

(Option C)

  • Life expectancy at birth: A positive mortality indicator· Average no. of years a newborn is expected to live, considering the current age-specific mortality rates in a community.
  • Important component to calculate the Human Development Index (HDI).
  • Life expectancy at one year is PQLI. In 2021, life expectancy in India is 69.7 years.

Infant mortality rate

IMR = (Total number of deaths (0-1-year-old) in a given year / Total number of live births in the same year) x 1000. It is a health status indicator.

Under-five mortality rate

U5MR = (Total number of deaths (0-5 years old) in a given year /Total number of live births in one year) x 1000

Maternal Mortality Rate

Maternal Mortality Rate (MMR) = (Total no. of maternal deaths/women in the reproductive age group [15-49 years]) x 100,000

Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR)

Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) = (Total no. of maternal deaths/Live Births) x 100,000

Adult mortality rate

Probability of dying between 15 to 60 years of life

Year of potential life lost (Option D)

Premature death measurement. If life expectancy is 75 years, and death happens at age 30, then 45 years of potential life is lost

Proportional mortality rate (Option B)

The simplest measure of the burden of disease (Total deaths due to disease 'x'/ Total deaths in a community)́ x 100

Case fatality rate

CFR = (Deaths due to diseases ‘z’ / total no of cases of disease ‘z’) x 100

questions.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman with a history of mechanical mitral valve replacement was on therapeutic low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) during her pregnancy. Her last dose of LMWH was administered 12 hours ago and she is currently due for delivery after 7 days. What is the most appropriate management plan for anticoagulation in this patient ?

options.label: A
options.text: Proceed with vaginal delivery without stopping LMWH and continue therapeutic dosing postpartum

options.label: B
options.text: Administer protamine sulfate to reverse the effects of LMWH before delivery

options.label: C
options.text: Transition from LMWH to unfractionated heparin 1 week prior to delivery

options.label: D
options.text: Proceed with cesarean delivery to avoid complications related to anticoagulation

questions.answerText: Transition from LMWH to unfractionated heparin 1 week prior to delivery
questions.solution: an class="customMeta" data-dictid="b2df2436bf1692777193d90e9c0132">molecular weight heparin is to be replaced with unfractionated heparin 1 week prior to delivery as it has a faster action and easy reversibility. Transition to unfractionated heparin (UFH) 1 week prior to labor or planned delivery is the preferred approach in patients requiring anticoagulation during pregnancy. UFH has a shorter half-life and is easier to reverse than LMWH, allowing flexibility in managing labor and delivery Anticoagulation increases the risk of maternal hemorrhage during delivery. Stopping anticoagulation too early increases the risk of thromboembolism , especially in high-risk patients like those with mechanical valves. LMWH has a longer half-life and if labor begins before LMWH clears, there may be complications with bleeding or the inability to place regional anesthesia safely. Unfractionated heparin (UFH) is preferred near delivery because: It has a shorter half-life (~1.5 hours). It can be stopped 4–6 hours before delivery or reversed with protamine sulfate if needed. Anticoagulation is resumed postpartum after assessing bleeding risk. Proceeding with vaginal delivery without stopping LMWH and continuing therapeutic dosing postpartum (Option A) increases the risk of uncontrolled hemorrhage thus it should not be done. Administration of protamine sulfate to reverse the effects of LMWH before delivery (Option B) partially reverses LMWH but is not routinely used unless there is significant bleeding and moreover reversal of anticoagulation therapy increases the risk of thromboembolism in high risk patients Proceeding with cesarean delivery to avoid complications related to anticoagulation (Option D) is not done as Cesarean delivery is not indicated solely due to anticoagulation unless there are obstetric or fetal indications. Vaginal delivery is the preferred mode of delivery for most women with heart disease, as it poses less hemodynamic stress. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
an class="customMeta" data-dictid="b2df2436bf1692777193d90e9c0132">molecular weight heparin is to be replaced with unfractionated heparin 1 week prior to delivery as it has a faster action and easy reversibility.

 

Transition to unfractionated heparin (UFH) 1 week prior to labor or planned delivery is the preferred approach in patients requiring anticoagulation during pregnancy. UFH has a shorter half-life and is easier to reverse than LMWH, allowing flexibility in managing labor and delivery

  • Anticoagulation increases the risk of maternal hemorrhage during delivery.
  • Stopping anticoagulation too early increases the risk of thromboembolism, especially in high-risk patients like those with mechanical valves.
  • LMWH has a longer half-life and if labor begins before LMWH clears, there may be complications with bleeding or the inability to place regional anesthesia safely.
  • Unfractionated heparin (UFH) is preferred near delivery because:
    • It has a shorter half-life (~1.5 hours).
    • It can be stopped 4–6 hours before delivery or reversed with protamine sulfate if needed.
  • Anticoagulation is resumed postpartum after assessing bleeding risk.

Proceeding with vaginal delivery without stopping LMWH and continuing therapeutic dosing postpartum (Option A) increases the risk of uncontrolled hemorrhage thus it should not be done.

Administration of protamine sulfate to reverse the effects of LMWH before delivery (Option B) partially reverses LMWH but is not routinely used unless there is significant bleeding and moreover reversal of anticoagulation therapy increases the risk of thromboembolism in high risk patients

Proceeding with cesarean delivery to avoid complications related to anticoagulation (Option D) is not done as Cesarean delivery is not indicated solely due to anticoagulation unless there are obstetric or fetal indications. Vaginal delivery is the preferred mode of delivery for most women with heart disease, as it poses less hemodynamic stress.

questions.solution: /strong> Explanation: Caudal epidural anaesthesia is a common practice in paediatric age groups . It involves the insertion of a needle or catheter through the sacrococcygeal ligament, which covers the sacral hiatus formed by the un-fused laminae of S4 and S5. It is frequently employed for procedures located below the diaphragm , such as urogenital, rectal, inguinal, and lower extremity surgeries. In adults , it is employed for anorectal procedures , as it provides dense sacral sensory blockade with minimal upward spread . Spinal anaesthesia (Option A) involves injecting anaesthetic into the cerebrospinal fluid but is generally not preferred for young children due to risks of hypotension and prolonged motor blockade. questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the role of the phase difference between the oval and round windows in sound transmission?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following best describes the role of the phase difference between the oval and round windows in sound transmission?

options.label: A
options.text: It amplifies sound waves by 10 dB

options.label: B
options.text: It prevents the cancellation of sound waves, allowing perilymph movement

options.label: C
options.text: It ensures simultaneous vibration of the oval and round windows

options.label: D
options.text: It decreases sound transmission efficiency, reducing hearing sensitivity by 4 dB

questions.answerText: It prevents the cancellation of sound waves, allowing perilymph movement
questions.solution: p> Explanation: The phase difference between the oval window (which receives sound vibrations from the stapes) and the round window is crucial in preventing the cancellation of sound waves. The oval window receives compression waves, while the round window experiences the rarefaction phase, allowing proper movement of the perilymph in the cochlea. Without this phase difference, sound waves reaching the two windows at the same time would cancel each other out, leading to no movement of the perilymph and ineffective sound transmission. It amplifies sound waves by 10 dB (Option A): The phase difference between the oval and round windows contributes to sound transmission but does not amplify sound by 10 dB. The actual contribution of the phase difference to hearing sensitivity is about 4 dB, not 10 dB . It ensures simultaneous vibration of the oval and round windows (Option C) : The oval and round windows do not vibrate simultaneously. In fact, their non-simultaneous movement is what prevents the cancellation of sound waves and ensures proper movement of the perilymph. It decreases sound transmission efficiency, reducing hearing sensitivity by 4 dB (Option D): The phase difference between the oval and round windows actually enhances sound transmission efficiency and contributes to increasing hearing sensitivity by about 4 dB , not decreasing it. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
p>

Explanation:

  • The phase difference between the oval window (which receives sound vibrations from the stapes) and the round window is crucial in preventing the cancellation of sound waves.
  • The oval window receives compression waves, while the round window experiences the rarefaction phase, allowing proper movement of the perilymph in the cochlea.
  • Without this phase difference, sound waves reaching the two windows at the same time would cancel each other out, leading to no movement of the perilymph and ineffective sound transmission.

 

It amplifies sound waves by 10 dB (Option A): The phase difference between the oval and round windows contributes to sound transmission but does not amplify sound by 10 dB. The actual contribution of the phase difference to hearing sensitivity is about 4 dB, not 10 dB.

 

It ensures simultaneous vibration of the oval and round windows (Option C): The oval and round windows do not vibrate simultaneously. In fact, their non-simultaneous movement is what prevents the cancellation of sound waves and ensures proper movement of the perilymph.

 

It decreases sound transmission efficiency, reducing hearing sensitivity by 4 dB (Option D): The phase difference between the oval and round windows actually enhances sound transmission efficiency and contributes to increasing hearing sensitivity by about 4 dB, not decreasing it.

The kidney transplant surgery proceeds as planned, but within minutes of reperfusion, the kidney becomes mottled, cyanotic and anuric. What is the cause for this presentation?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease recently received a compatible donor organ from her brother. The kidney transplant surgery proceeds as planned, but within minutes of reperfusion, the kidney becomes mottled, cyanotic and anuric. What is the cause for this presentation?
questions.solution: lass="customMeta" data-dictid="c7c23b05e116927771899b5232b3d7">hyperacute graft rejection due to preformed antibodies in the recipient. Hyperacute Graft Rejection Hyperacute Graft Rejection is the most rapid and catastrophic form of graft rejection, occurring immediately on the operating table or within the first 48 hours of transplantation. Pathogenesis: Hyperacute rejection is caused by preformed circulating IgG antibodies against donor antigens (mainly HLA or ABO), which may arise from prior pregnancies, multiple blood transfusions, or previous organ transplants. Mechanism: Preformed antibodies bind to donor endothelial antigens, activating complement and causing widespread thrombosis, vascular occlusion, ischemia, and graft necrosis, leading to a kidney that rapidly becomes cyanotic, flaccid, and anuric (sometimes with a few drops of blood). Clinical features: Hyperacute rejection presents with a mottled blue ischemic kidney, loss of graft tone, and absent urine output (anuria) or occasionally hematuria (few drops of blood). Immunologically, hyperacute rejection represents a Type II hypersensitivity reaction mediated by antibodies . @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
lass="customMeta" data-dictid="c7c23b05e116927771899b5232b3d7">hyperacute graft rejection due to preformed antibodies in the recipient.

Hyperacute Graft Rejection

  • Hyperacute Graft Rejection is the most rapid and catastrophic form of graft rejection, occurring immediately on the operating table or within the first 48 hours of transplantation.
  • Pathogenesis: Hyperacute rejection is caused by preformed circulating IgG antibodies against donor antigens (mainly HLA or ABO), which may arise from prior pregnancies, multiple blood transfusions, or previous organ transplants.
  • Mechanism: Preformed antibodies bind to donor endothelial antigens, activating complement and causing widespread thrombosis, vascular occlusion, ischemia, and graft necrosis, leading to a kidney that rapidly becomes cyanotic, flaccid, and anuric (sometimes with a few drops of blood).
  • Clinical features: Hyperacute rejection presents with a mottled blue ischemic kidney, loss of graft tone, and absent urine output (anuria) or occasionally hematuria (few drops of blood).
  • Immunologically, hyperacute rejection represents a Type II hypersensitivity reaction mediated by antibodies.
